questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two targets that cannot both hold
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to present two targets that cannot both hold
questions.stem: A projection note asks how two conflicting targets can sit on one sheet.

options.text: It must mark the conflict explicitly, because projecting both as attainable misrepresents the choice
It should show the reduction target alone, since it is the stricter measure and settles the question
options.misconception: assumes the stricter target always binds on its own

options.text: It should shade both regions without comment, since the reader can see the tension for themselves
options.misconception: assumes the reader will notice and resolve a hidden conflict

options.text: It should average the two targets, because a compromise figure is the only honest way to draw a line
options.misconception: believes averaging removes rather than conceals a trade-off

questions.explanation: When two targets cannot both hold, the map must say so rather than imply both are reachable. Drawing one without comment, or averaging them, hides a real decision about which constraint binds.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader would wrongly conclude.

questions.topic: What a permanent fabric change does to demand
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a permanent fabric change moves material demand
questions.stem: A projection note proposes testing how a lasting design change moves demand.

answer.exemplar: Give the class a product that uses 200 kg of material per unit and a set of alternatives, one using 150 kg, one using 120 kg and one using the same 200 kg. Ask them to calculate material demand at each service level of 10000 units and then to change the service level to 14000 units. The exercise should make clear that a permanent design change shifts the material used per unit, so demand changes even when the number of units sold does not, and should end with a rule for separating design effects from volume effects in any projection.

questions.explanation: Holding the number of units fixed isolates the design change, so demand moves with material per unit rather than sales. Changing the service level afterwards shows how the two effects separate.
questions.hint: Hold the number of units constant first.

questions.topic: Where the loop in a material system closes
questions.learningObjective: Identify how much recycled material re-enters production
questions.stem: A projection note reads a material flow diagram: 400000 tonnes of product were made, 320000 tonnes were collected for recycling, 250000 tonnes returned to production as feedstock, and of those 150000 tonnes were exported. How many tonnes re-entered production?

options.text: 320000 tonnes, because that is the figure for material collected for recycling in the year
options.misconception: uses the collected figure as if it closed the loop

options.text: 400000 tonnes, because every tonne produced eventually returns to the production line
options.misconception: assumes no material ever leaves the system

options.text: 100000 tonnes, because 150000 of the 250000 returned tonnes were exported instead
150000 tonnes, because the exported tonnes are the ones that re-entered production
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the exported flow

questions.explanation: Of the 250000 tonnes that returned as feedstock, 150000 were exported rather than used, so 100000 tonnes re-entered production. The collection figure counts what was gathered, not what closed the loop.
questions.hint: Subtract the exported tonnes from those returned.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Which stream sets the strictest handling rules
questions.learningObjective: Explain which waste stream usually sets the strictest handling rules
questions.stem: A projection note asks which layer of the waste map carries the tightest rules.

answer.exemplar: The most tightly controlled stream is usually the one that concentrates the greatest hazard in the smallest quantity, such as a concentrate of heavy metals, a solvent or a component containing a persistent compound. Regulators set the strictest rules there because exposure is per unit of volume rather than per unit of tonnes handled, so a small tonnage can carry a disproportionate share of risk. Reading the strictness of a stream therefore tells you where control effort, monitoring frequency and liability should concentrate, rather than where the largest mass sits.

questions.explanation: The strictest stream usually holds concentrated hazard in a small tonnage, so rules target exposure per unit rather than mass. Severity of handling tells you where control effort belongs.
questions.hint: Ask what is concentrated rather than what is heavy.

questions.topic: Why a mean cannot close a site
questions.learningObjective: Test whether a site mean can support a closure decision
questions.stem: A projection note asks about a contaminated site: the average concentration across the site is 40 milligrams per kilogram, but the worst 5 percent of the area measures 900. Can the site be closed on the mean?

options.text: Yes, because the mean is the fair summary of the whole site and closure is judged on the average
options.misconception: treats the average as the closure test

options.text: Yes, because the worst 5 percent is too small a fraction of the site to affect the decision
options.misconception: treats a small area as irrelevant to a site-wide decision

options.text: No, because the mean hides the worst area and closure depends on the worst area being safe
No, because the mean is always too conservative for any closure decision anywhere
options.misconception: overstates the rule into a universal prohibition

questions.explanation: The mean of 40 sits far below the 900 found in the worst area, so the average conceals the ground that matters most. Closure depends on the worst area being safe, not on the average.
questions.hint: Ask what the worst area looks like.

questions.topic: Why a closure bond is required before the last tonne
questions.learningObjective: Explain why closure assurance must precede the last shipment
questions.stem: A projection note asks why a bond is drawn before the last tonne moves.

options.text: Because a bond can only be issued once the site has been fully remediated and handed back
options.misconception: reverses the timing of the instrument

options.text: Because the bond replaces the need to monitor the site for the required period afterwards
options.misconception: confuses financial assurance with monitoring duties

options.text: Because regulators cannot inspect a site until the closure bond has been paid out in full
options.misconception: links inspection rights to the payout of the bond

options.text: Because the money must exist before the operator can walk away with the funds already spent

questions.explanation: A bond guarantees money for work still to come, so it must exist before the operator's obligations end. Posting it after remediation would leave nothing to enforce against if the site failed its checks.

questions.topic: A target no inspection can verify
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an absolute target using its surrogate records
questions.stem: A projection note examines an absolute target: a city generates 200000 tonnes of waste a year, 140000 tonnes are diverted and 60000 tonnes are landfilled. What diversion rate does this show, and what can it evidence?

options.text: 30 percent, since landfill takes 60000 of the 200000 tonnes each year
options.misconception: reads the landfilled share as the diversion rate

options.text: 85 percent, since recycling and composting together remove more than two thirds of the waste
options.misconception: estimates the rate without using the given tonnages

options.text: 70 percent, since 140000 of the 200000 tonnes are already kept out of landfill
100 percent, because the target of zero landfill means diversion is already complete
options.misconception: reads the target itself as the achieved result

questions.explanation: Diversion is the share kept out of landfill, so 140000 over 200000 gives 70 percent, matching the 30 percent still landfilled. An absolute target can only be audited through such surrogates, since absence cannot be inspected directly.
questions.hint: Divide the diverted tonnage by the total produced.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two targets that cannot both hold
questions.learningObjective: Test two conflicting targets against each other on a map
questions.stem: A projection note proposes a test of conflicting targets on one sheet.

answer.exemplar: Take two targets for one region, a 40 percent cut in material sent to landfill and a 30 percent rise in material re-use, and map the current state of both at ward level so the tension is visible. Run the two scenarios separately and then together, recording for how many wards the targets can both be met, and mark the wards where they collide with the population affected. Finally, let learners try the averaged compromise line and ask what it hides. The exercise should end with a statement of which target binds and where, rather than a single figure for the region.

questions.explanation: Mapping both targets at ward level shows where the collision sits and who is affected. Running the scenarios separately and together separates a genuine conflict from a modelling artefact.
questions.hint: Map both targets and find where they collide.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a permanent fabric change does to demand
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a permanent change to use shifts material demand
questions.stem: A projection note asks what a lasting material change does to the demand curve.

answer.exemplar: A permanent change to the way a material is used shifts the demand curve rather than moving along it, because the change alters what the material is for rather than what it costs. Where the new use displaces the old one, demand for virgin material falls and demand for recycled material may rise, so total tonnage can shrink as the mix shifts. Where the new use adds a service that did not exist, total tonnage rises instead, and the recycled share depends on how collection and sorting are arranged. Reading the direction of the change in total tonnage is therefore the first task for any projection.

questions.explanation: A permanent change to use shifts the demand curve itself, and total tonnage falls or rises depending on whether the new use displaces the old one or adds to it. The recycled share then depends on collection and sorting.
questions.hint: Ask whether the new use replaces the old one.

options.text: Because household refuse is collected weekly while electronics are collected only on request
options.misconception: explains separation by collection frequency

questions.explanation: Separating electronics keeps concentrated metals and hazardous components out of mixed refuse, where they would be dispersed and lost. The aim is capture of specific materials, not tidier logistics.

options.misconception: judges the sites by their averages rather than their worst areas

options.text: Site one, because its worst area of 120 is three times the threshold while site two's is under double
Neither, because the threshold applies to the mean of each site rather than to the worst area

options.text: Site one, because a lower mean makes any single high reading more significant in itself
options.misconception: reasons from the mean rather than the reading

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a closure bond is required before the last tonne
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of closure financial assurance
questions.stem: A projection note proposes a way to test closure financial assurance.

answer.exemplar: Give learners a site with a remediation plan of four phases and a total cost, and a scenario in which the operator's funds are depleted after phase two. Ask them to draw the point at which the site becomes unfinishable without external money, and then to position the bond, the sinking fund and the step-in agreement around that point. Finally, give them a case where the bond was only posted after the last shipment and ask them to explain who ends up carrying the cost. The exercise should end with a rule that financial assurance precedes irreversible physical work.

questions.explanation: Locating the point where the site becomes unfinishable shows why assurance must precede irreversible work. The late-posting case makes clear who carries the cost when protection is arranged too late.
questions.hint: Find the point where the site becomes unfinishable.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A target no inspection can verify
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an absence target cannot be inspected directly
questions.stem: A projection note asks why some targets can never be inspected directly.

answer.exemplar: An absence such as zero emissions or zero waste to landfill cannot be observed at the thing itself, because there is nothing there to point a camera at, so no inspector can confirm it by looking. The evidence has to come from surrogates: the fuel purchased by the plant, the weight of material recorded at the weighbridge, the throughput of the treatment plant, and the consistency between those records. Verification therefore depends on the quality of the indirect evidence and on how completely the records cover the activity, which is why the coverage of the records, not the wording of the target, determines whether it can be audited.

questions.explanation: An absence leaves nothing at the site to inspect, so verification rests on indirect records and their coverage. Auditability is a property of the record keeping, not of the wording of the target.
questions.hint: Ask what the inspector could actually look at.

options.misconception: assumes the larger loss of uses always dominates

options.text: Market two, because the larger material increase per use dominates the smaller loss of uses
options.misconception: assumes the larger material increase always dominates

questions.topic: Why electronics are separated from refuse
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of electronics collection routes
questions.stem: A projection note proposes comparing two collection routes.

answer.exemplar: Give the class two equal tonnages of household waste, one mixed and one in which electronics have been removed at source, and ask them to value the recoverable metals in each. Finally, let them model a take-back route for electronics and compare its recovery with the separate collection result. The exercise should end with a stated reason why the stream is separated rather than merely recovered.

questions.explanation: Valuing the two equal tonnages shows what mixing destroys, and modelling the downstream treatment cost prices that loss. Comparing with a take-back route shows which route actually recovers the value.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a mean cannot close a site
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a site average can report but not decide
questions.stem: A projection note asks why reporting by average falls short at closure.

answer.exemplar: A site average is useful for reporting because it gives a single figure that can be compared between sites and tracked over time, which is what most public reporting needs. It cannot carry a closure decision because closure turns on whether every part of the ground meets the standard, and averaging divides the effect of one hot area across the whole site. A site can pass comfortably on the average while a small patch of ground remains far above the standard and still requires treatment, and that patch is where people and water actually meet the site.

questions.explanation: An average gives a comparable reporting figure but spreads a hot area across the whole site. Closure is a statement about every part, so the average cannot carry it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a small hot area in the mean.

answer.exemplar: Give learners a flow diagram with quantities at every node for one material, from extraction through use, collection, sorting and reprocessing, and ask them to account for every collected tonne: reprocessed into production, exported, stored, contaminated or discarded. questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Which stream sets the strictest handling rules
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the strictness of handling rules should be set
questions.stem: A projection note asks how to grade the waste layers.

answer.exemplar: Handling rules should follow the hazard carried per unit of material, the behaviour of that hazard in the environment, and the number of people or ecosystems likely to come into contact with it. Tonnage is a poor guide because a small stream of highly concentrated sludge can carry more risk than a large stream of mixed refuse spread over a wide area. Setting rules by mass would then load the cost onto the largest stream, which is usually the cleanest, while the genuinely dangerous fraction is handled under the least demanding regime.

questions.explanation: Rules should track hazard and exposure rather than mass, because concentrated small streams carry disproportionate risk. Grading by tonnage misprices the risk and under-regulates the dangerous fraction.
questions.hint: Ask what is concentrated rather than what is heavy.

answer.exemplar: A permanent change in fabric or design appears as a shift in the level of material demand, because the same service is now delivered with a different quantity of material or the material is used for a different purpose. It is misread in two directions. If material intensity falls, the drop in tonnage looks like a cyclical softening and is expected to reverse, when it will not. If the change creates a new use, the rise looks like economic growth, so that when the new use saturates the projection is badly wrong. questions.stem: A projection note compares two districts claiming zero landfill: district one has weighbridge records covering 96 percent of its waste, and district two has records covering 61 percent, with the rest estimated. Which claim is better supported?

options.text: Neither, because an absolute target can never be supported by indirect records of any completeness
options.misconception: denies that indirect evidence can ever support a claim

options.text: District two, because an estimate with a stated method is better than a partial measured record
options.misconception: prefers an estimate to a measured record

options.text: Both equally, because both districts have declared a target of zero and the declaration is what counts
options.misconception: treats a declaration as equivalent to evidence

options.text: District one, because its records cover nearly all the waste while the other's estimates leave a large gap

questions.explanation: The completeness of the underlying records decides how well an absence claim can be supported, and district one covers 96 percent of its waste against 61 percent. A declared target is intent, not evidence.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the waste the records actually cover.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two targets that cannot both hold
questions.learningObjective: Test whether a conflict is arithmetic or a matter of timing
questions.stem: A projection note proposes dating the measures in a conflict test.

answer.exemplar: Give learners a region with two targets, a 40 percent cut in material sent to landfill and a 30 percent rise in material re-use, and let them map the current state at ward level. Then ask them to schedule the measures over ten years, with each measure dated, and to find the year in which the two targets can first be met together on a given ward. Learners should then remove one measure and see which ward fails and when. The exercise should end with a rule that a conflict on today's map is a statement about timing, not about the arithmetic of the targets.

questions.explanation: Dating each measure and finding the first year both hold shows that a conflict can be a timing problem rather than an arithmetic one. Removing one measure shows which ward fails and when.
questions.hint: Date the measures and look for the first feasible year.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a permanent fabric change does to demand
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a permanent change shifts rather than moves along demand
questions.stem: A projection note asks how a permanent change redraws the demand curve.

answer.exemplar: A permanent change to how a product is made changes the quantity of material the same service needs, so the demand for that material moves to a new level rather than sliding along the existing curve. A price change or a rise in output moves a buyer along a curve that already exists; a design change redraws the curve because the product now contains less or more material for the same job. Reading the shift as a movement along the curve would assume the old relationship still holds, and any projection built on that assumption would fade back towards the old tonnage as volumes grew.

questions.explanation: A design change redraws the demand curve because the same service now needs a different quantity of material. Reading it as movement along the curve would fade any projection back towards old tonnages.
questions.hint: Ask whether the relationship itself has changed.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Where the loop in a material system closes
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of production met by recycled material
questions.stem: A projection note computes one year of a loop: 1000000 tonnes of product were made, 600000 tonnes were collected, 450000 tonnes were reprocessed into usable feedstock, and 380000 tonnes of that went back into production while 70000 were exported. Give the percentage of production met by recycled material.
questions.explanation: Recycled material met 380000 of the 1000000 tonnes of production, which is 38 percent. The collection and reprocessing figures are intermediate steps and would overstate the loop if used in their place.
questions.hint: Divide recycled input by total production.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Which stream sets the strictest handling rules
questions.learningObjective: Grade three streams and match rule sets to their hazard
questions.stem: A projection note sets out three streams and their rule sets: 1200 tonnes of solvent waste, 250 tonnes of heavy metal sludge and 90000 tonnes of food waste. Which combination of strictness and rule set is defensible?

options.text: The sludge needs the strictest rules for hazard, the solvent a controlled route, and food waste the lightest
Food waste needs the strictest rules, because it degrades fastest and creates the greatest odour load
options.misconception: grades strictness by decomposition speed rather than hazard

options.text: The solvent can be treated as ordinary refuse, because its hazard is diluted once mixed with other waste
options.misconception: assumes dilution removes the hazard from a stream

options.text: All three need identical rules, because a single uniform standard is simpler to apply and to inspect
options.misconception: assumes one uniform rule set fits every stream

questions.explanation: Grading by hazard per tonne makes the metal sludge the most severe and food waste the least. The rule sets then follow: strictest handling for sludge, a controlled route for solvent and the lightest for food waste.
questions.hint: Grade by hazard, not by mass.
